name: Nasal dilator / strips

lead: Nasal strips and internal dilators are adhesive or insert devices that hold the nostrils open. They are used for congestion, sleep and snoring.
In looksmaxxing communities they are sometimes discussed in connection with jaw or face development; they affect airflow in the moment and are not reported to change facial structure.

paras: A spring-like strip across the nose lifts the nasal side walls and stiffens the nasal valve, lowering airflow resistance while worn.

Side effects are mostly adhesive skin irritation. A systematic review found no significant change in apnea-hypopnea index or snoring index in sleep apnea, so they are not a treatment for it. Benefits for congestion or snoring in people without apnea are mostly subjective.

lead: Nasal dilators are devices that hold the nostrils or nasal valve open to ease airflow. External dilator strips are adhesive bandages with embedded plastic ribs or splints, applied across the bridge and sides of the nose, while internal dilators are inserted into the nostrils [1][2]. They are sold over the counter and used for nasal congestion, snoring, sleep and exercise [1].

In looksmaxxing discussions, nasal breathing is sometimes linked to facial development and appearance, and strips are occasionally mentioned in that context. Dilators act on airflow while worn; none of the sources reviewed reports that they change facial structure.

Systematic reviews report that external strips do not improve exercise performance measures such as maximal oxygen uptake [3], and a 2016 systematic review of dilators in snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea is on record [4]. Reported side effects are mainly skin irritation from the adhesive [1].
infobox: External adhesive strip or internal nostril insert
Late 1980s by Bruce Johnson; patent filed 1990, per Grokipedia [2]
FDA 510(k) clearance reported for October 1993, Class I device [2]

paras: An external nasal strip is a flexible adhesive band with parallel plastic bands inside that act like a spring across the nasal valve, the narrowest part of the nasal airway. Grokipedia describes standard human strips as roughly 1.5 to 2 cm wide and 5 to 7 cm long, made from layered non-woven or film substrate with pressure-sensitive skin adhesive [2]. Internal dilators, by contrast, sit inside the nostrils; examples studied in the literature include Nozovent and a newer device called Nas-Air [5][6].

A related veterinary product exists for horses, which breathe only through the nose. Wikipedia says the equine strip was invented by two veterinarians, James Chiapetta and Edward Blach, in the 1990s, and is intended chiefly to reduce exercise-induced pulmonary haemorrhage rather than to improve performance [1].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports that the modern human strip was developed in the late 1980s by Minnesota product designer Bruce Johnson as a remedy for his own congestion from a deviated septum, that he filed a patent in 1990 (granted 1996), and that CNS Inc. licensed it in 1992 and sold it as Breathe Right [2]. It also reports FDA 510(k) clearance in October 1993 as a Class I device for over-the-counter use, and a surge in popularity in the mid-1990s as American football players wore the strips, including during Super Bowl XXIX in 1995 [2]. These details come from an unverified AI-generated source. The same source mentions a 1905 device by George Francis for detecting nasal obstruction by dilating the nostrils [2].

During inhalation the soft side walls of the nose are pulled inward by negative pressure. Wikipedia explains that strips adhere to the skin and hold the anterior nasal aperture open so that it does not collapse, lifting and widening the passage [1]. A 2006 Rhinology review of mechanical alar dilators concluded that devices such as Breathe Right and Nozovent dilate the nasal valves, reduce nasal resistance and improve airflow, mostly during inspiration, that responses vary greatly between individuals, and that the effect may be lower in non-Caucasians [5]. One study cited by Wikipedia found that strips widen the front part of the nasal cavity but not the posterior part [1].

Exercise: a 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of external nasal dilator strips in sport included 19 eligible articles; for maximal oxygen uptake in 168 participants it found no statistically significant difference [3]. A 2022 meta-analysis examined dilators and physiological parameters of running performance [7]. Randomized trials have also looked at endurance athletes and adolescent athletes [8][9].

Congestion: a randomized clinical trial published in the American Journal of Rhinology in 2005 is titled as reporting that opening the nasal valve with external dilators reduces congestive symptoms in healthy subjects [10]. A 1999 study reported that strips increase maximum inspiratory flow by stabilising the nasal wall [11].

Snoring and sleep: a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis examined Breathe Right strips and Nozovent for snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea [4]; its pooled results are reported to show no significant change in apnoea-hypopnoea index or snoring index in sleep apnoea. A 2006 randomized trial of 80 non-obese adults with chronic sleep-maintenance insomnia and mild to moderate sleep-disordered-breathing symptoms compared four weeks of strips (n=42) with a control (n=38) on validated insomnia and sleep quality scales [12]. A trial of the internal Nas-Air device in 41 outpatients who snore assessed snoring duration [6]. A 2022 study examined strips and sleep-disordered breathing measures in pregnancy [13]. Strips have also been proposed and examined as a placebo comparator in CPAP trials [14]. A 2016 systematic review compared over-the-counter mechanical dilators [15].
No study in the sources reviewed tests dilators for any effect on facial structure or aesthetics.

Wikipedia states that strips have no reported side effects other than possible skin irritation from the adhesive [1]. A systematic review reported no significant effect of dilators on apnoea-hypopnoea index in sleep apnoea, so they are not described as a treatment for that condition [4]. Persistent nasal obstruction, loud snoring with daytime sleepiness, or witnessed pauses in breathing are conventionally evaluated medically rather than managed with strips.

Strips and internal dilators come up in discussions of nasal versus mouth breathing during sleep and exercise. Proponents of nasal breathing connect it with facial development, and strips are sometimes suggested as a way to encourage it; the evidence reviewed shows the devices affect airflow only while worn [5]. Their benefits for people without sleep apnoea are mostly reported subjectively.

Products differ in strip strength, size, adhesive type and whether they are external or internal. Reviews of over-the-counter dilators have compared designs [15]. Typical prices are around $10 to $25 for a box.

timeline.event: Bruce Johnson reportedly files a patent for the adhesive nasal strip, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia [2].
CNS Inc. is reported to license the invention and market it as Breathe Right [2].
FDA 510(k) clearance is reported for October 1993 [2].
Strips become widely visible among football players, including at Super Bowl XXIX, according to the same source [2].
